lead: Electric power is made in a few large plants and used in millions of small places. The layout of generation, transmission and distribution is the chain of transformers and lines that joins the two: generate at 11–25 kV, step up for the long run, step down at substations, and step down once more to 400 V near the load. The reason is loss. A higher voltage means a smaller current for the same power, and line loss falls with the square of the current.
prereq: You need: three-phase star and delta connections and line/phase values (see Unit 2, Single-Phase and Three-Phase AC Circuits) and the transformer working principle (see Unit 3, Magnetic Circuits and Electrical Machines).

sections.h3: Why the voltage goes up and down

blocks.text: A plant generator produces 11 kV to 25 kV. Homes and shops need 230 V, often 200 km away. Sending 11 kV that far turns most of the power into heat in the line. So the voltage is raised at the plant, carried high, and lowered in steps near the load.

blocks.where: P is the total three-phase active power in W; V_L is the line-to-line voltage in V; I_L is the line current in A; cos φ is the power factor.

blocks.text: P_loss = 3 I_L² R = R P² / (V_L² cos²φ)
blocks.where: P_loss is the total heat lost in all three line conductors in W; R is the resistance of one conductor in Ω; the other symbols are as above.

blocks.text: The loss falls as the square of the voltage. Doubling V_L halves I_L and divides the loss by four. At 400 kV the line loss is a small fraction of the power sent; at 11 kV it would be a large share. This is why long-distance transmission is never done at the generator voltage.

items: Generation: the alternator produces 11–25 kV. Building it for 400 kV would need insulation that cannot be cooled and far costlier windings.
Step-up transformer: raises the voltage to 400 kV, 220 kV or 132 kV. The current falls by the same ratio, so a thinner conductor carries the same power.
Transmission line: carries power to the city. Standard AC levels in India are 765 kV, 400 kV, 220 kV, 132 kV and 66 kV; 66 kV is subtransmission in some regions.
Step-down substations: 400/220 kV, then 220/66 kV, then 66/33 kV, then 33/11 kV. Each one feeds a smaller area than the one before.
Primary distribution: 11 kV lines run along the roads on poles to each neighbourhood.
Distribution transformer: 11 kV/400 V, mounted on a pole or in a small yard, one per street or building block.
Consumer: receives 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase.

blocks.text: The 11 kV and 400 V networks are usually radial, meaning one path with no loop back. Protection is then simple, but one fault can darken a whole street.

items: Incoming 11 kV feeder, overhead or underground, with an isolator and a circuit breaker.
11 kV busbar: a metal bar that feeds several transformer bays.

Transformer: primary winding in delta on the 11 kV side, secondary in star with the neutral brought out. The delta lets triplen harmonic currents circulate inside it, so they do not reach the line voltages; the star point can be earthed.
400 V LT busbar: receives the secondary. Three phases and a neutral leave it.
Outgoing feeders: each street gets a fuse-switch unit or an MCB, and live, neutral and earth run to the consumer.

blocks.text: The star secondary gives two voltages. Between any two phases the line voltage is 400 V. From one phase to the neutral the phase voltage is 400 / √3 = 231 V, written 230 V. A single-phase load goes between one phase and the neutral; a three-phase motor goes on all three phases plus earth.

Current transformers on the 11 kV side feed an overcurrent relay that trips the breaker. On the 400 V side the MCBs do the same job street by street. Earthing the star point holds the neutral near earth potential (see 6.8).
A single-line diagram (SLD) draws a three-phase circuit as one line, because all three phases normally behave alike. It is the drawing an engineer checks before switching.

items: Transformer: two interlocked circles, with Δ or Y written beside them.
Circuit breaker: a small square. Isolator: a diagonal line (knife switch), often drawn open. It has no arc-quenching, so it is opened only after the circuit breaker has cleared the current.
Rating beside each item: 11 kV/400 V, 100 kVA, 50 Hz.

Read from source to load, checking the voltage at every step. Voltage rises once, at the step-up transformer, and then falls at every step-down substation and at the distribution transformer. A rise where a step-down is expected means an arrow or a winding symbol is reversed.

figure.caption: Power leaves the generator at 11–25 kV, is raised for the long run, and is brought down in stages to 230/400 V at the consumer. The local 11 kV/400 V transformer is the last step before the meter.

spec.title: Generation to consumer
spec.aria: A generator feeds a step-up transformer, a high-voltage transmission line, step-down substations including 33/11 kV, an 11 kV feeder and a local 11 kV/400 V transformer before the consumer.

examples.question: A distribution transformer rated 100 kVA, 11 kV/400 V, 50 Hz supplies a balanced three-phase load at 0.8 power factor lagging. Find the line current on the 400 V side, the line current on the 11 kV side, and the active and reactive power drawn by the load.
steps: Check turns ratio: 11000 / 400 = 27.5, and 144.34 / 5.25 = 27.5. Currents are inverse to voltages.
Q = S sin φ = 100 × 0.6 = 60 kVAR, since sin φ = 0.6 when cos φ = 0.8.
examples.answer: The 400 V side carries 144.34 A per line and the 11 kV side 5.25 A per line, while the load draws 80.0 kW and 60.0 kVAR.
examples.check:
import math
S = 100e3
V_lv = 400.0
V_hv = 11000.0
pf = 0.8
I_lv = S / (math.sqrt(3) * V_lv)
I_hv = S / (math.sqrt(3) * V_hv)
P = S * pf
Q = S * math.sqrt(1 - pf**2)
print(round(I_lv, 2))
print(round(I_hv, 2))
print(P / 1000)
print(Q / 1000)

traps: 400 V is the line voltage of the three-phase four-wire supply and 230 V is the phase voltage: 400 / √3 = 231 V, rounded to 230 V. A single-phase consumer gets one phase and the neutral, never 400 V.
A transformer changes voltage and current, not power. 100 kVA in at 11 kV is 100 kVA out at 400 V minus small loss; the currents are in inverse ratio to the voltages.
In P_loss = 3 I_L² R the 3 counts the three phase conductors. Writing I²R alone for a three-phase line gives one third of the true loss.
Generation is at 11–25 kV, not at 220 kV. The step-up transformer sits between the generator and the line; saying the generator produces 220 kV is a standard exam error.
The distribution transformer is the last one in the chain, 11 kV/400 V. The transformer at the plant or grid substation is a power transformer.

quiz.q: Name the stages of the power layout in order and give the usual voltage at each.
quiz.a: Generation at 11–25 kV, step-up to 400/220/132 kV, transmission at that level, step-down substations to 66/33 kV and then 11 kV, primary distribution at 11 kV, distribution transformer 11 kV/400 V, consumer at 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase.

quiz.q: Why is power sent at high voltage instead of at the generator voltage?
quiz.a: For the same power, I_L = P / (√3 V_L cos φ), so raising the voltage lowers the current. The loss is 3 I_L² R, so it falls as the square of the voltage. Less loss also means a thinner, cheaper conductor for the same power.

quiz.q: A 200 kVA, 11 kV/400 V transformer works at full load. Find the line current on each side.
An 11 kV feeder delivers 200 A at unity power factor over 5 km. Each conductor has 0.3 Ω/km. Find the line loss. Find the loss if the same power were sent at 33 kV through the same conductors.
quiz.a: R = 0.3 × 5 = 1.5 Ω per conductor. P = √3 × 11000 × 200 = 3810.5 kW. Loss = 3 × 200² × 1.5 = 180 kW. At 33 kV, I = 3810500 / (1.7321 × 33000) = 66.67 A, so loss = 3 × 66.67² × 1.5 = 20 kW. Three times the voltage gives one ninth of the loss.

quiz.q: Why is the secondary of a distribution transformer star connected with the neutral brought out?
quiz.a: The star point gives a neutral. Line voltage is 400 V and phase voltage is 400 / √3 = 231 V, so both single-phase and three-phase loads can be supplied. The star point can also be earthed, which keeps the neutral near earth potential.

quiz.q: A single-line diagram shows an 11 kV bus, a transformer, a 400 V bus, a fuse and a cable to a house. Explain what each symbol tells you and where the MCB belongs.
quiz.a: The thick bars are busbars at 11 kV and 400 V. The two circles are the transformer stepping 11 kV down to 400 V. The fuse protects one outgoing street feeder; the MCB belongs at the consumer end, in the distribution board, backed by the fuse or a breaker at the substation.

quiz.q: State the relation between line and phase voltage for a star-connected secondary.
quiz.a: V_L = √3 V_ph. With V_L = 400 V, V_ph = 400 / √3 = 231 V, written 230 V. The line current equals the phase current in star.

beyond: Not for the exam. The whole country runs as one synchronous grid at 50 Hz, and load dispatch centres balance generation against demand minute by minute. Where AC cables would lose too much, high-voltage DC links join regions instead. SCADA and smart meters let a control room watch a substation's current and voltage live. Rooftop solar has made the low-voltage network two-way, so an 11 kV/400 V transformer sometimes sees power flow backwards. Search for 'single-line diagram', 'load dispatch centre' or 'HVDC back-to-back' to go further.
